boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Fort Stevens record (July 11-12, 1864) in Early's Raid and Operations Against the B&O Railroad [June-August 1864]. The July 10 march from Frederick and the July 13 withdrawal are context. Campaign-wide marches, levies, captures, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Divisions; the live field reads zero. Early says his infantry did not exceed 10,000, Breckinridge's (nominally much larger) not over 2,500 muskets. Pond quotes Barnard that about 20,400 men were available, of whom only 9,000, mostly raw, garrisoned the defences, and he lists later arrivals: the Sixth Corps put 900 men on picket, Meigs reported 1,500 armed employees and Price 2,800 convalescents. He says 800 men of Emory's division arrived with the Sixth Corps.
claims.rationale: Early's figure is his own statement of infantry; the Union figures are availability, garrison and arrival counts at different times of July 10-11, not the force engaged on July 12. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Early says the fortifications were very strong: inclosed forts connected by breastworks, with ditches, palisades and abatis, every approach swept by artillery cross-fire including heavy guns. Pond names Fort Stevens in Early's front, De Russy to the west and Slocum to the east, and says the Rives house on rising ground, with shade trees and an orchard, covered the Confederate sharpshooters.
claims.rationale: The works existed when Early arrived, per both accounts, and are tagged inherited for this engagement; the Rives house cover was occupied during it. No map verification.

claims.value: Early says his men marched thirty miles on July 10 in heat and dust, that on the 11th many fell out and the rest arrived almost completely exhausted, and that with troops gathering around him he would find it difficult to get supplies. He reports over 1,000 horses brought off and $220,000 levied at Hagerstown and Frederick. Pond says men fell by the wayside, exhausted and half suffocated.
claims.rationale: Interested and retrospective descriptions of condition, not a readiness measure; the levy and horses are campaign totals.

claims.value: Early says it became apparent before his assault that the enemy had been strongly reinforced and that he knew the Sixth Corps had arrived. Pond says Early knew from prisoners that troops had been sent from Grant's army and saw troops filing into the works. Wright, at 4.10 p.m. on the 11th, believed the enemy near Fort Stevens only a very light skirmish line. Early says Northern reports greatly exaggerated his force.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from interested accounts and a history; no message log inspected.

claims.value: Early decided on withdrawal after consulting his division commanders. Pond says Augur had placed the collected troops in the forts with McCook in command, that Wright held his corps in reserve subject to McCook's orders, and that on July 12 Wright pushed out Bidwell's brigade, which advanced at a sign from Wright on the parapet. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Early and Major Generals Horatio G. Wright and Alexander McDowell McCook; the live page lists Wright and Early (as Major General) only.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report and a history; no listed commander receives automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory and the live result Union Victory. Pond says the July 12 attack expelled Early's skirmishers from the Rives house and drove his pickets back a mile; Early says his reinforced skirmishers repulsed the enemy three times, and that he retired after night in entire good order and without loss.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 874 total; the live field reads 873 (US 373; CS 500). Pond gives the attacking brigade a loss of 250 and 280 for the force engaged on July 12, Hardin's division 73 killed and wounded over the two days, and the total Union loss in the demonstration between 400 and 500; he says about 30 Confederate dead and 70 seriously wounded were left behind. Early's report gives no loss for July 11-12.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: McCook's, Wright's, Hardin's, Wheaton's and the other defence-of-Washington reports, Chipman's status report, Fitts's statement of Confederate strength and Rodes's July reports remain deferred; Wallace's reports (selected for MD007) are not used here.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office and field despatches; it quotes the reports of the commanders it describes and is not independent of them. Early's July 14, 1864 report to Lee, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVII, Part 1, is one interested Confederate family; Pond quotes it. The Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
